Each black dot represents one biological replicate (WT: n = 6; Setdb1 cKO: n = 3). Data were combined across three independent experiments for WT and two independent experiments for Setdb1 cKO. Bars indicate means. Significance was assessed using Welch’s unpaired t-test, P = 0.007. d, Separation scores for the HC and EC regions of the locus. In the schematic, red regions represent heterochromatin and grey regions represent euchromatin. e, HC domain size as a fraction of total locus volume in terms of Rg. For d and e, distributions are shown as violin plots. Horizontal lines and numbers indicate medians. Significance was assessed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Adjusted P values for Rad21 cKO versus WT, WT versus Setdb1 cKO and Rad21 cKO versus Setdb1 cKO, respectively: P = 1.5 × 10−103, P = 3.6 × 10−101 and P < 1 × 10−230 in d and P = 1.1 × 10−23, P = 2.3 × 10−71 and P = 2.6 × 10−229 in e. **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. f, ORCA traces from each condition with the heterochromatin domain and Pcdh enhancers labelled. g, Percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh gene across genotypes. Pcdhb1 is excluded.h, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the HS5-1 enhancer in Rad21 cKO relative to WT. i, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the heterochromatin domain boundary determined by nChIP–seq at the Pcdha cluster in Setdb1 cKO relative to WT.

Individual traces reflected these structural changes. Single molecules demonstrated distancing of Pcdh enhancers from the heterochromatin domain in Rad21 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by changes in the distance of each locus position relative to the heterochromatin domain centre (Extended Data Fig. 10d). Meanwhile, the heterochromatin domain seemed less compact and more intermixed with euchromatin in Setdb1 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by an increase in the entropy of each locus position in Setdb1 cKO (Extended Data Fig. 10e). These data suggest that Pcdh enhancers require cohesin to approach the heterochromatin domain and contact target promoters, whereas heterochromatin keeps the promoters in a compact and ordered environment.

To evaluate how these changes in Pcdh locus architecture affect stochastic Pcdh gene expression, we performed single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq). Ablation of Rad21 resulted in widespread downregulation of Pcdh expression in favour of Pcdhac2, the Pcdha gene most proximal to the HS5-1 enhancer, which also resides in euchromatin (Fig. 5g,h and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). This gain in expression of enhancer-proximal Pcdh genes was not observed at the Pcdhg cluster, suggesting distinct enhancer–promoter specificities at the two clusters (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). By contrast, ablation of Setdb1 resulted in upregulation of Pcdha10–12 and Pcdhgb6–b7, the genes closest to the heterochromatin–euchromatin boundaries at the locus (Fig. 5g,i and Extended Data Fig. 10f,h). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies reflected these expression changes in both genotypes (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j).

Sources indicate that these results indicate that DNA loop extrusion and heterochromatin compaction cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote an unbiased enhancer–promoter search space at the locus. While cohesin is required for Pcdh enhancers to gain access to the heterochromatin domain housing Pcdh promoters, the compaction of the domain expands the ability of the enhancers to find target promoters. Thus, although generally viewed as antagonistic processes35, both cohesin and heterochromatin-driven chromatin compartmentalization are indispensable for proper Pcdh expression.

According to recent reports, here we show that heterochromatin spatially partitions the Pcdh locus into a compacted domain housing Pcdh promoters and multiple open regions housing Pcdh enhancers. Transcription from chosen promoters occurs within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Counterintuitively, Pcdh transcription can read through hundreds of kilobases without dissolving the compacted state of the locus (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We further demonstrate that Pcdh locus architecture and proper Pcdh expression are achieved through cooperation between heterochromatin-mediated compaction and cohesin-mediated DNA loop extrusion.

According to recent reports, our findings challenge the prevailing view that heterochromatin is a physically inaccessible chromatin structure. Heterochromatin compaction was initially proposed to sterically hinder the transcriptional machinery and thereby repress gene expression36,37. However, rather than acting as an impenetrable barrier, our data indicate that heterochromatin can support active transcription while retaining a compact 3D organization. These findings add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that heterochromatin is not intrinsically inaccessible and can support transcription. For example, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-dense centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin are actively transcribed and accumulate abundant RNA despite their highly condensed appearance38. Furthermore, transcription can stabilize H3K9me3-modifying enzymes39,40,41, and dense heterochromatin nonetheless allows passage of transcription factors42 and large macromolecules43, including RNA polymerase II (ref. 44).

Industry observers note that these observations have motivated an alternative model of heterochromatin organization, wherein domain-scale compaction emerges from frequent intra-domain interactions that serve to reinforce the epigenetic state of the domain rather than directly silence the underlying DNA through steric exclusion. By this model, distal genomic loci are brought into proximity by the activity of heterochromatin reader and writer proteins, as readers bound to heterochromatin marks on one chromatin fibre might promote deposition of the same modification by writers on another fibre. This 3D reader–writer activity establishes a positive feedback loop that reinforces the heterochromatic state of the domain. Heterochromatin compaction thus functions to concentrate this feedback, ensuring it acts primarily back on the existing heterochromatin to stabilize its epigenetic state, rather than spreading or diluting to neighbouring euchromatin45,46.

Although heterochromatin has been proposed to be important for epigenetic memory at the Pcdh locus11,12, we found that chosen Pcdh promoters do not segregate from flanking promoters retaining the silent state, contrasting with the behaviour of chosen promoters in H3K27me3 heterochromatin29,47. This unexpected organization argues against domain-scale spatial segregation as a primary mechanism for heterochromatin-mediated memory of Pcdh gene choice. Instead, these data suggest that a more local compartmentalization of active and inactive genes might develop, with biophysically distinct microcompartments, or ‘pockets’, of active chromatin containing expressed genes forming within the heterochromatin domain. This model is consistent with the presence of both highly dynamic and more stable HP1 populations within the same heterochromatin environment48 and structural heterogeneity of heterochromatin compartments, as revealed by recent single-molecule footprinting49 and chromatin tracing46 studies.

In a recent development, lastly, beyond classical examples of heterochromatic genes, such as the lt and rl genes in Drosophila3,4,5, the intermixed spatial organization of active and inactive genes within H3K9me3-enriched chromatin domains discussed here may reflect a more general property of gene regulation within heterochromatic territories—with particular relevance to genes arranged in clusters, such as OR6 and KZFP genes7. We propose that domain-scale spatial segregation of active and inactive genes might not be required at these clusters to accommodate and maintain expression of subsets of genes within a more broadly repressive chromatin domain. Furthermore, as we have shown here for Pcdh genes, these loci might also require the coordinated integration of genome folding mechanisms across scales—from higher-order heterochromatin compartmentalization to enhancer–promoter interactions mediated by various looping factors50—to achieve genomic architectures required for precise and selective gene activation.

In summary, our findings illustrate how seemingly silent chromatin domains can coordinate gene expression and invite a reconceptualization of heterochromatin from a singularly repressive chromatin environment to one that can, when properly configured, permit active transcription.

Mice were treated in compliance with the rules and regulations of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of California, San Francisco under the IACUC protocol AN-170364-03F. For ORCA experiments involving RNA imaging, postnatal day 11 mice were used. For ORCA experiments involving conditional knockouts, mice older than postnatal day 35 were used to allow time for the knockout to take effect. Rad21 cKO mice were generated by crossing Rad21 conditional allele mice51 to Omp-ires-cre mice (Omptm1(cre)Jae) harbouring a Cre-inducible tdTomato allele (ROSA26-tdtomato, Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J). Setdb1 cKO mice were generated using the same strategy. Setdb1 conditional allele mice were purchased from Shanghai Model Organisms (C57BL/6Smoc-Setdb1tm1(flox)Smoc, NM-CKO-190052). For the nChIP–seq experiments, cells were sorted from Krt5–GFP (labelling HBCs), Ngn1–GFP (labelling INPs) and Omp-ires–GFP (labelling mOSNs) mice. Primers used for genotyping mice are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

According to recent reports, mice were perfused with 30 ml of ice-cold PBS followed by 30 ml of freshly prepared, ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Tissue from the mouse OE was dissected and incubated in 4% PFA with gentle rocking at 4 °C for 6 h. Tissue was then transferred to 30% sucrose in 1 × PBS, incubated with gentle rocking at 4 °C until sunk, then embedded in OCT. For ORCA experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 6 μm onto glass coverslips (Biooptechs, 40-1313-03191) coated with chromium potassium gelatin. Slides were coated as described previously52. For immunohistochemistry experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 20 μm onto Superfrost Plus slides (Fisherbrand, 1255015). ORCA coverslips were stored at −80 °C until use; immunohistochemistry slides were stored at −20 °C until use.

Sources indicate that for a breakdown of all ORCA-related experiments in the present study, see Supplementary Table 4. The genomic coordinates of the ORCA barcodes tiling the Pcdh locus are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

RNA and DNA probes were designed and hybridized as previously described52, with minor modifications as follows. Briefly, for combined RNA/DNA imaging experiments, RNA probes were hybridized and imaged first. Tissue sections mounted on coverslips were fixed in freshly prepared 4% PFA at room temperature for 10 min, followed by three washes in 1 × PBS. Sections were then permeabilized for 10 min at room temperature in 1% Triton X in 1 × PBS, followed by two washes with 1 × PBS. Next, sections were incubated for 5 min at room temperature in a protease solution consisting of 0.1 mg ml−1 pepsin (Sigma Aldrich, 501784863) in 10 mM HCl and washed twice in 0.1 M glycine in 1 × PBS to improve RNA hybridization efficiency. Sections were then cleared in 8% sodium dodecyl sulfate at room temperature for 10 min and washed three times in 2 × SSC, reducing background fluorescence. Following clearing, sections were incubated in Hybridization Buffer (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 0.1% Tween) for 35 min at room temperature. Then, 2,500 ng of primary RNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 10% dextran sulfate, 0.1% Tween) were added to the sections, covered with coverglass and incubated overnight (12–20 h) at 42 °C. The following morning, samples were washed twice for 10 min in 2 × SSC at 42 °C, washed once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then imaged. After RNA imaging, samples were re-fixed in 4% PFA for 5 min at room temperature, washed three times in 2 × SSC, re-permeabilized for 10 min in 1% Triton X-100 at room temperature and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Sections were subsequently incubated for 5 min in 0.1 M HCl and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Pre-hybridization was performed for 35 min as for RNA, then 5,000 ng of DNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution were added to sections and covered with coverglass. Sections were then incubated on a 90 °C hotplate for exactly 7 min and transferred to 42 °C overnight. The following morning, samples were washed twice in 2 × SSC for 10 min at 42 °C, once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then incubated in a post-fix solution (2% glutaraldehyde, 8% PFA in 1 × PBS) for 30 min. Samples were then washed three times in 2 × SSC and imaged.

For ORCA experiments not involving RNA imaging, samples were fixed, permeabilized, cleared, treated with HCl, pre-hybridized and hybridized as described above, but omitting the protease step. Inclusion of the protease step was found to substantially improve RNA staining and was therefore used only for experiments that included RNA imaging. For ORCA experiments involving fluorescent protein labelling (for example, tdTomato signal in Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO), samples were first fixed and washed, imaged for the fluorescent protein and then processed for DNA ORCA as described above. Throughout all procedures, care was taken to prevent sections from drying at any point in the protocol to minimize tissue shrinkage between RNA or protein imaging rounds and subsequent DNA imaging rounds.

Samples hybridized with primary probes were imaged on a previously described custom microscopy and microfluidics setup29,52. RNA and DNA readout barcodes were labelled sequentially with a 750 dye complementary to the readout barcodes on primary probes. All RNA and DNA probes share a common sequence that was labelled with a Cy3 dye complementary to this sequence, referred to as the fiducial. Fiducial probes were added before the first imaging round and imaged alongside each barcode. Fiducial signal was subsequently used for drift correction and alignment across imaging rounds. For RNA imaging, the fiducial signal captures all stained RNAs, whereas for DNA imaging it appears as discrete puncta, with each punctum representing one Pcdh locus.

OE tissue was first stained for H3K9me3 as follows. Tissue on glass coverslips was fixed for 10 min in 4% PFA, washed twice in 1 × PBS, quenched for 5 min in PBS containing 0.1 M glycine and washed again in PBS. Tissue was permeabilized with three 5-min washes in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then blocked in PBS containing 1% BSA and 200 U ml−1 RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs, M0314L). Primary antibody incubation was performed overnight at 4 °C using rabbit anti-H3K9me3 antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Abcam, ab8898). The following morning, tissue was washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then incubated with donkey anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 647 secondary antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, A31573). Tissue was then washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100. Samples were stored at 4 °C in PBS protected from light until imaging. To image OE tissue with STORM, an imaging buffer was prepared immediately before use as follows. A dilution buffer was first prepared containing 50 mM NaCl and 200 mM Tris pH 8.0. A glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution was prepared by combining 700 μl of dilution buffer, 49 mg of glucose oxidase and 175 μl of catalase, centrifuging at maximum speed for 1 min and collecting 800 μl of supernatant. STORM imaging buffer was prepared by adding 800 μl of glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution, 8 ml of 50% glucose and 400 μl of β-mercaptoethanol to 32 ml of dilution buffer.

For each field of view, fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample immediately before imaging. H3K9me3 STORM videos were acquired at five axial positions using the 635-nm laser at maximum power and an exposure time of 0.5 s per frame. The first and fourth videos contained 3,000 frames, whereas the remaining videos contained 2,500 frames. Fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample after the third video to maintain fluorophore blinking during prolonged imaging. Further frames were acquired after addition of fresh buffer because extra illumination time was required for photobleaching before robust fluorophore blinking could be observed.

It has been revealed that STORM videos were acquired across multiple axial planes rather than using astigmatism-based 3D STORM with a cylindrical lens53, because high tissue background made accurate fitting of astigmatic spot widths unreliable. The five axial planes were separated by 750 nm and sampled a 3.0-μm axial range centred on the plane with strongest H3K9me3 signal. Subsequent ORCA imaging of the same samples was acquired using Z-stacks containing matched axial planes to those imaged by STORM.

Fluorescently tagged WGA, which labels cell membranes, was used to align fields of view across imaging sessions (for example, to align H3K9me3 STORM, RNA and Pcdh DNA images). First, 3 μl of 1 ng μl−1 WGA was diluted in 600 μl of 2 × SSC, added to samples for 15 min, then washed off with 2 × SSC immediately before imaging. For RNA and Pcdh DNA imaging, the fiducial channel was imaged alongside the WGA signal at the end of each imaging session. For H3K9me3 STORM, WGA images for each field of view were taken immediately following completion of STORM acquisition. For imaging of fluorescent proteins tagging mOSNs, WGA was imaged simultaneously in a different channel alongside the fluorescent protein. When aligning images across RNA and DNA imaging rounds, images from each field of view were first aligned to the fiducial signal acquired with WGA, and fields of view were subsequently registered across imaging modalities using the WGA signal. The WGA signal additionally enabled 3D cell segmentation (described below).

All imaging was performed on a custom microscopy and microfluidics setup as previously described29,52. The details of the microscopy setup are also listed on the 4DN data portal and Mirco-Meta App54 under Stanford-Boettiger_lab_ORCA_Nikon_Eclipse_Ti2-U_Scope3.

It has been revealed that three-dimensional cell segmentations were generated from the WGA signal acquired during RNA imaging. We trained a Cellpose55 algorithm to identify cell outlines in individual sections of WGA images. This algorithm was then run on every section of WGA Z-stack images for each field of view. To connect the resulting two-dimensional (2D) cell segmentations into 3D cell segmentations, we applied ultrack56, an algorithm initially designed to track cells over time in time-series data, to the 2D segmentations for each stack, effectively treating the Z dimension as time. Ultrack produced 3D cell segmentations that matched WGA staining (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We used ultrack, as we found Cellpose’s performance with 2D images to be superior to its performance with 3D images for OE sections stained with WGA.

Recent findings suggest that segmented cells were classified into distinct cell types on the basis of RNA transcripts within each segmentation as follows. RNA puncta were first identified from 3D stacks using storm-analysis (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7679267), which identifies their X, Y position in each frame and is robust to overlapping spots. The Z position of each punctum was computed by fitting the axial fluorescence intensity profile to puncta with a common X, Y position (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7698979). RNA puncta were then mapped to cell segmentations and segmentations were classified by cell type as follows: for each cell, counts of Icam1, Ascl1, Tex15, Gap43 and Omp transcripts were log-transformed, Z-scored and combined into marker-specific scores corresponding to HBCs (Icam1), GBCs (Ascl1), INPs (Tex15), iOSNs (Gap43) and mOSNs (Omp high, Gap43 low). Cells were assigned to the cell type with the highest score, subject to further marker-based rules (Tex15+ cells were forced to INP and not allowed to be mOSN; HBC labels were forbidden in Gap43+ or Omp+ cells). A confidence score was defined as the difference between the top two scores, and cells with low confidence or ambiguous profiles were labelled ‘undetermined’. To map DNA loci to each segmentation, the X, Y, Z coordinates of DNA loci were transformed by the image alignments computed between WGA images. Each locus was then mapped to a classified cell from its respective field of view and assigned that cell’s label.

For ORCA experiments involving protein rather than RNA staining, DNA loci were classified as belonging to a particular cell type (namely, mOSNs) on the basis of the fluorescent signal of tdTomato. Apart from Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e, data in all figures come from cells classified as mOSNs.

After aligning images from RNA and DNA imaging rounds, the X, Y, Z positions of RNA puncta and DNA loci were registered into a common coordinate system. For each DNA locus, we computed the 3D Euclidean distance to every RNA punctum in the same field of view in voxel units, where X–Y coordinates are in pixels and Z is in imaging planes. A locus was classified as ‘transcribing’ for a given gene if at least one RNA punctum for that gene lay within a 3D distance of 8 voxel units, and as ‘non-transcribing’ otherwise. This threshold corresponds to 1.23–1.60 μm in physical space, depending on how the separation between DNA and RNA puncta is distributed across the X–Y and Z axes. The threshold of 8 voxel units was chosen on the basis of the distribution of nearest RNA distances across all DNA loci for each Pcdh RNA, which was consistently bimodal, with one population less than 8 voxel units and another greater than or equal to 8 voxel units.

In a recent development, STORM videos were processed frame by frame using the 2dfixed multi-emitter-fitting algorithm from storm-analysis (https://github.com/ZhuangLab/storm-analysis). Initial frames dominated by saturated fluorescence before photobleaching were excluded. Single-molecule localizations in each frame were identified using a 10-sigma detection threshold and fit with a fixed-width 2D Gaussian model using an initial Gaussian sigma of 1.3 pixels. Drift correction was not applied during fitting. Localizations were fit independently for each axial imaging plane, and each localization was assigned the Z position of its corresponding imaging plane for downstream analysis.

H3K9me3 STORM signal around Pcdh loci in mOSNs was quantified as the number of STORM localizations within a 324-nm radius, corresponding to 3 pixels, of the X–Y position of the fiducial signal of each locus. Similar results were obtained using different radius sizes. For each locus, localizations were counted from the STORM imaging plane or planes nearest to the locus in Z. If the locus was located in the same Z plane as a STORM video, only localizations from that plane were used. If the locus was located between two STORM imaging planes, localizations from both planes were included and linearly weighted according to their proximity to the locus Z position. For example, for a locus located at Z plane 26 between STORM videos acquired at planes 25 and 28, localizations from plane 25 were weighted by 2/3 and localizations from plane 28 were weighted by 1/3. For the analyses in Fig. 2f, the same quantification was performed using the X, Y and Z position of the ORCA barcode containing the Pcdh gene being analysed, rather than the fiducial position of the locus.

Recent findings suggest that for the simulations in Fig. 2c, randomized positions were used to compare H3K9me3 STORM signal at observed Pcdh loci with signal expected at other positions within the same nuclei. For each of 1,000 simulations, one random position was selected for each observed Pcdh locus from the same cell and Z plane, thereby controlling for non-uniform axial distribution of H3K9me3 STORM signal within individual cells. H3K9me3 STORM signal was quantified at each randomized position using the same 324-nm radius and Z-plane weighting scheme described above. The median STORM signal from each simulation was used to generate a null distribution, which was compared with the observed median STORM signal around Pcdh loci to calculate an empirical P value. The same randomization and quantification procedure was performed for putative Tex15 transcription sites in INPs for Extended Data Fig. 7d. Putative Tex15 transcription sites were identified from Tex15 RNA FISH z-stacks by detecting bright 3D regional maxima. For each field of view, the Tex15 stack was smoothed with a 3D Gaussian filter and thresholded to identify local maxima corresponding to candidate nascent RNA puncta. The intensity threshold was empirically chosen by visual inspection across fields of view to retain bright Tex15 transcription sites while excluding dimmer spots probably corresponding to mature transcripts.

Recent findings suggest that for visualization of H3K9me3 STORM localizations together with ORCA traces in three dimensions (Extended Data Fig. 7a), STORM localizations from each axial imaging plane were shown with a randomized Z position drawn from a truncated Gaussian distribution centred on the corresponding STORM imaging plane. The Gaussian had a standard deviation of 1.2 imaging-plane units and was truncated to ±3.5 imaging-plane units around the plane centre. This jittering was used only to create smooth 3D renderings of STORM signal across the sparsely sampled axial planes and was not used for quantitative analyses.

Image processing (drift correction and localization of spots) was performed as described previously29,52 using ORCA analysis tools (https://github.com/BoettigerLab/ORCA-public).

Sources indicate that before downstream analyses, ORCA traces were quality filtered on the basis of barcode detection. For each experiment, we computed the number of detected barcodes per trace. Median barcode detection per trace was calculated to be around 40–60 barcodes, and we restricted our analysis to traces with ≥25 detected barcodes. We further filtered out traces with unnaturally high barcode detection, keeping only traces with ≤86 barcodes detected. For each retained trace, the 3D positions of detected barcodes were ordered by genomic position. Next, barcodes with consistently poor detection or abnormal labelling (for example, failed strand displacement) were assigned estimated positions by linear interpolation in traces for which the immediately flanking barcodes were detected. This selective interpolation was applied to 2–5 barcodes per experiment. For contact frequency map analyses, such as those presented in Figs. 1e and 3e–g, we further interpolated missing barcodes using a maximum gap length of three consecutive missing barcodes. This interpolation preserved the major features of contact frequency maps while improving their smoothness. Different maximum gap lengths were tested. Gap lengths greater than three did not produce measurable further smoothing, whereas allowing larger interpolations produced abnormally short adjacent-barcode distances. For all other analyses, raw detected barcode positions were used, with only the selective interpolation of poorly labelled barcodes described above.

For contact frequency analyses, we chose contact thresholds near the average distance between adjacent barcodes in a spatially contiguous region of the locus. These thresholds ranged from 170 to 220 nm across experiments. We also conducted a threshold parameter sweep to verify that observed contact patterns were robust to a range of thresholds around the selected value, and varying the contact threshold within a reasonable range did not qualitatively alter any within-experiment effects. Thresholds were used to call contacts between all barcode pairs in an experiment. The thresholds used for each experiment are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

It has been revealed that enhancer–promoter barcode pairs were assigned on the basis of previously reported regulatory relationships between Pcdh cluster enhancers and their target promoters13,15,25,57, together with the ORCA locus positions containing the corresponding genes and enhancers. All Pcdha genes were assigned the HS5-1 enhancer (barcode 27), whereas Pcdhb genes were assigned the HS18-22 enhancer (barcode 78) and Pcdhg genes were assigned the HS16-17 enhancer (barcode 76). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies were extracted from contact frequency matrices generated from max-gap-3 interpolated polymer coordinates, as described above. For ORCA barcodes containing multiple Pcdh promoters, combined gene labels were used.

We defined the geometric centre of an ORCA trace as the median X, Y, Z position of all detected barcodes in that trace. For the distance-to-centre profiles in Fig. 1i, we computed the Euclidean distance between each barcode and this centre on a per-trace basis, then plotted, for each position, the median distance across all traces. When distances to the centre of the heterochromatin domain were measured in Fig. 4c and Extended Data Figs. 9a–d and 10d, the heterochromatin centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned to the heterochromatin domain (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67), and the distances of relevant locus positions to this centre were measured. When distances to the centre of a euchromatin region were measured in Extended Data Fig. 9a–d, the centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned either to the euchromatin stretch between the Pcdha and Pcdhb clusters (barcodes 15–28) or to the euchromatin stretch downstream of the Pcdhg cluster (barcodes 68–90), depending on the specific locus position being analysed.

Radius of gyration (\({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\)) was used as a single-number measure of the spatial spread of a set of barcodes around its geometric centre47. For a set of \(N\) barcodes with 3D coordinates {\({r}_{i}\)}, we first calculated the centre \(c\) as the coordinate-wise median position, then defined \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) as \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}{\sum }_{i=1}^{N}{||}{r}_{i}-c{{||}}^{2}}\). The \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) of the heterochromatin domain was primarily evaluated. In Fig. 5e, the heterochromatin domain \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) was calculated as a fraction of the trace-wide \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\).

For each isoform measured in Fig. 4a, the promoter barcode was assigned on the basis of the ORCA locus position containing the respective Pcdh gene. The heterochromatin compartment was defined as barcodes 2–14 and 29–67. The euchromatin compartment was defined on the basis of the cluster of the promoter being analysed: barcodes 15–28 for Pcdha promoters, and barcodes 68–90 for Pcdhb and Pcdhg promoters. The promoter barcode itself was excluded from the compartment to which it belonged. For each trace, a promoter-to-heterochromatin centre distance was calculated as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all heterochromatin compartment barcodes. Promoter-to-euchromatin centre distances were calculated analogously as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all barcodes in the corresponding euchromatin compartment.

In Extended Data Fig. 10e, entropy was calculated for the distance distributions between pairs of locus positions as described previously58. For each barcode pair, we pooled 3D distances across all traces within each genotype separately, then normalized each genotype’s distances by that genotype’s own median distance for the pair to account for length-scale differences between experiments. We then pooled the normalized distances from both genotypes together and set common histogram bin edges (50 bins) using the 1st and 99th percentiles of this pooled, normalized distribution, so that entropy values were computed on the same scale for both genotypes. Using these shared bin edges, we separately estimated each genotype’s distribution, normalized bin counts to probabilities pk and computed Shannon entropy as \(S=-{\sum }_{k}{p}_{k}{\log }_{2}({p}_{k})\), such that higher S reflects broader, more variable distances and lower S indicates more narrowly peaked, reproducible distances. For each locus position, we calculated its entropy with respect to all other positions, averaged these pairwise entropies per position and compared the resulting mean entropies between Setdb1 cKO and WT.

Industry observers note that to quantify spatial segregation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the Pcdh locus, we calculated a separation score as follows. For each polymer, we designated heterochromatin locus positions (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67) as region A and euchromatic locus positions (barcodes 15–28 and 68–90) as region B, computed all pairwise 3D distances and took the median distance between A and B (heterochromatin–euchromatin) and the median distance within A (heterochromatin–heterochromatin). The separation score was defined as the ratio of these two medians (medianA–B/medianA–A), such that higher values indicate that the heterochromatin domain is more spatially separated from neighbouring euchromatin. This score was computed per trace for WT, Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO and compared across genotypes.

Recent findings suggest that to validate the specificity of RNA probes targeting Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms, plasmids encoding Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons fused to mCherry under control of a CMV promoter were generated through FastCloning59. Plasmid sequences were validated using Plasmidsaurus. Plasmids were transfected into Cath.a-differentiated cells grown in eight-well Ibidi glass-bottom plates (Ibidi, 80827). Cells were seeded at a density of 40,000 cells per well in 220 μl of media and transfected after 24 h of growth using lipofectamine (Invitrogen, L3000001). Each well was then stained with primary RNA probes according to the procedure described above. For 12 plasmids across each of the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, three wells were transfected, with each well stained by a different ORCA readout barcode. Only wells that were labelled with a readout barcode mapping to the Pcdh isoform they were transfected with produced signal.

FACS isolation of mouse OSNs was performed as previously described15. In brief, mice were euthanized with CO2 followed by cervical dislocation and OE tissue was immediately dissected. Cells were then dissociated into a single-cell suspension by incubating freshly dissected tissue with papain for 30–40 min at 37 °C according to the Worthington Papain Dissociation System. After dissociation and filtering through a 35-μm cell strainer, cells were resuspended in 1 × PBS with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), DNase (0.0025% final concentration) and DAPI. Fluorescent cells were sorted on a FACS Aria Fusion cell sorter (BD Biosciences) with BD FACSDiva 9.0.1 software. Cells were sorted into 1 × PBS + 2% FBS. FACS gating strategies used to isolate GFP+ and tdTomato+ mOSNs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

According to recent reports, scRNA-seq experiments were performed as previously described15. In brief, cells were dissociated from OE tissue from 4- to 5-week-old mice as described above. About 70,000 mOSNs were FACS-isolated. Complementary DNA and library preparation were performed using the 10x Genomics Single Cell 5′ Gene Expression workflow, and libraries were sequenced using a NovaSeq SP100 PE50 and a NextSeq 2000 P2 200 through the UCSF Gladstone Genomic Core and the UCSF Center for Advanced Technology. Sequencing data were processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger 6.0.1. Data analysis was performed using Seurat60,61 and custom scripts. Cells were filtered to retain cells with 1,000–10,000 detected genes and less than 5% mitochondrial reads. Counts were then normalized using Seurat’s NormalizeData with log normalization and a scale factor of 10,000. See Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 for further details on scRNA-seq analysis and statistics.

For analyses in Fig. 5 and Extended Data Fig. 10, Pcdh isoform choice was analysed in mOSNs defined by detected Omp expression and no detected Gap43 expression using raw unique molecular identifier counts. A Pcdh isoform was considered detected in a given mOSN if one or more unique molecular identifier-corrected reads were assigned to that gene. For each condition, the percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh isoform was calculated as the fraction of mOSNs with detected expression of that isoform. Changes in Pcdh choice across genotypes were calculated as percentage-point differences relative to WT. Data for single-cell experiments represent one biological replicate per condition.

Sources indicate that nChIP–seq was performed as previously described62. Briefly, live cells were sorted from papain-dissociated mouse OE; in experiments for which spike-ins were included to enable quantification of ChIP signal across conditions, HEK293T cells at around 70% confluency were trypsinized, washed with PBS and added at a ratio of 0.75% to the sorted mouse cells. (HEK293T cells were grown in RPMI or DMEM media supplemented with 10% FBS and 1 × penicillin-streptomycin, incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO2, and tested for mycoplasma (ATCC Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit) before use in experiments.) Live sorted cells were pelleted in a swinging bucket centrifuge (800g, 15 min, 4 °C) and then resuspended in Buffer 1 (0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Cells were lysed on ice for 10 min by adding an equal volume of Buffer 2 (0.4% Igepal CA-630, 0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Nuclei were pelleted (1,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in MNase buffer (0.32 M sucrose, 4 mM MgCl2, 1 mM CaCl2, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Resuspended nuclei were treated with MNase (Sigma) at 37 °C, and the reaction was quenched with the addition of EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. Two fractions of solubilized chromatin were collected; nuclei were pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S1 was collected and stored at 4 °C overnight. Nuclei were resuspended in Dialysis Buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors) and rotated overnight at 4 °C. Insoluble material was pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S2 was retained. MNase treatment was optimized to yield predominantly mono-nucleosomes in the S1 fraction and predominantly di-nucleosomes, tri-nucleosomes and some larger chromatin fragments in the S2 fraction. S1 and S2 DNA concentrations were measured by HS DNA Qubit after RNase A treatment. Equal volumes of S1 and S2 fractions were pooled, and total yields were estimated. In spike-in experiments, chromatin input was not always equalized across immunoprecipitations, as spike-in normalization accounts for differences in input.

MNase-digested chromatin was diluted in Wash Buffer 1 (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10 mM EDTA, 125 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and 5% inputs were reserved. Histone H3 lysine 9 tri-methyl antibody (H3K9me3, Abcam ab8898) was added, and the binding reaction was rotated overnight at 4 °C. For each immunoprecipitation, 20 μl of Dynabeads Protein G (Invitrogen) were blocked overnight with 2 mg ml−1 yeast transfer RNA and 2 mg ml−1 BSA in Wash Buffer 1. The next day, blocked beads were added to antibody-bound chromatin and rotated for 1–3 h at 4 °C. Chromatin-bound beads were washed at 4 °C a total of four times with Wash Buffer I, three times with Wash Buffer II (5 mM Tris pH 7.5, 17.5 mM NaCl, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and one time with Tris-EDTA buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA). Two 15-min elutions were conducted at 37 °C in Elution Buffer (1% SDS, 250 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT). ChIP DNA and input DNA were column purified using Zymo ChIP DNA columns (Zymo Research, D5205 or D5201).

Libraries were prepared using the Ovation Ultralow V2 DNA-Seq Library Preparation Kit (Tecan Life Sciences). The quality of the libraries was assessed by Bioanalyzer and quantified using a combination of Bioanalyzer and Qubit. Libraries were pooled and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 (Gladstone Institutes), NextSeq 500/550 (UCSF Center for Advanced Technology) or NovaSeq X (Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Biohub San Francisco).

Data processing and analysis was conducted in accordance with previous literature63,64. For spike-in experiments, adapters were trimmed with cutadapt with --minimum-length 18 and checked for sequencing quality control with FastQC. Reads were aligned with Bowtie2 to a concatenated mouse and human genome (mm10 + hg38) in which the spike-in chromosomes were pre-labelled with a ‘_hg38’ suffix. Alignments were split by chromosome using bamUtil’s splitChromosome function, and samtools’ merge command was used to collect mouse and human alignments separately. Then, duplicates were marked and removed using Picard MarkDuplicates, and the spike-in chromosome suffix was stripped. Alignments with mapping quality < 30 were removed using samtools, and read counts aligning to the mouse and human genomes were used to calculate spike-in scaling factors.

As in the original ChIP-Rx method describing quantitative spike-in normalized ChIP followed by sequencing, our spike-in corrections normalized for the number of spike-in reads in the immunoprecipitation63. We sequenced every input as well, allowing us to adjust for the variability in spike-in read fraction in each input64,65. The spike-in adjusted coverage signal, \({z}_{i}\), was calculated from counts per million (CPM)-normalized coverage values, \({x}_{i}\), with the equation \({z}_{i}={x}_{i}\cdot \frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), where \({S}_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{in}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the inputs, respectively, and \({S}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the immunoprecipitations, respectively. Bigwig files were generated from Deeptools bamCoverage using --scaleFactor of \(\frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\cdot \frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), --binSize 10, --minMappingQuality 30 and --normalizeUsing CPM. In Fig. 5c, to compare spike-in-normalized nChIP–seq values from different experiments, we batch-corrected using the average of the scale factors from the WT samples within each experimental batch. Significance was assessed and confirmed using both a Welch’s unpaired t-test and a two-way ANOVA (main effects only).

For experiments without spike-ins, adapters were trimmed and the first 4 nucleotides of each read removed with cutadapt (v1.9.1; -u 4, --minimum-length 18). Reads were aligned to mm10 with Bowtie2. BigWig files were generated with deepTools bamCoverage in 10-base-pair bins from unextended reads, normalized to 1 × genome coverage (reads per genomic content; effective genome size 2,407,883,318; chr. X, chr. Y and chr. M excluded from normalization).

Sources indicate that immunohistochemistry for RAD21 was performed as described previously15. A similar staining protocol was performed for SETDB1, with minor modifications to the blocking buffer composition to improve signal. Sections were removed from −20 °C, washed in 1 × PBS for 5 min at room temperature, then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min. Sections were incubated in blocking solution (3% BSA, 0.2% Tween in 4 × SSC) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation proceeded overnight (12–16 h) at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. The following morning, sections were washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature, then incubated in secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Samples were then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature and mounted under coverslips with antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, H-2000-2). For RAD21 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:100 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, PA5-28344). For SETDB1 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:250 in blocking buffer (Thermofisher, MA5-47120). For both RAD21 and SETDB1, secondary antibody was added at 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen donkey anti-rabbit 647, A31573).

(a) Staining and classification strategy. mOSNs in OE sections from Omp-ires-Cre;tdTomatofl/fl mice were identified by imaging tdTomato signal prior to ORCA DNA labelling (left; scale bar: 20 μm). Pcdh DNA loci detected by ORCA (middle) were assigned as mOSN+ or mOSN- based on overlap with tdTomato signal (right). The OE is outlined. Representative images are shown from one experiment. tdTomato-based mOSN classification was performed in three independent ORCA experiments with similar results. (b) Comparison of ORCA contact frequency maps and Hi-C ligation frequency maps for the same genomic bins in mOSNs. (c) Pearson correlation between the ORCA contact frequencies and Hi-C ligation frequencies shown in (b). (d) Pearson r values for the correlation between ORCA contact frequencies and Hi-C ligation frequencies for different ORCA contact thresholds. (e) ORCA contact frequency maps from total OE in two separate wildtype mice. Locus positions corresponding to the Pcdha, Pcdhb, and Pcdhg clusters are labelled. Locus positions containing Pcdh enhancers are labelled with arrowheads. (f) Pearson correlation between contact frequencies from the biological replicates shown in (d). (g) Detection efficiency for each locus position imaged by ORCA from a representative experiment. For (b,d), n denotes the number of individual traces included in the analysis.

(a) Generation of 3D cell segmentations. OE sections were labeled with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA, left; scale bar: 20 μm). Cellpose was used to identify cell boundaries in individual 2D image slices (middle), and these segmentations were linked across Z to generate 3D cell volumes (right). (b) Classification of cell volumes by developmental stage. RNA puncta for marker genes were mapped to the 3D segmentations, and cells were assigned to OSN developmental stages based on marker-expression scores (right); only cells with high-confidence labels were used. (c) Pcdh DNA loci (left) were mapped to the classified 3D cell volumes and inherited the developmental-stage label of their containing cell (right). See Methods for more details.

For each trace, the corresponding single-molecule distance map reveals pairwise 3D distances between all imaged locus positions. Locus positions corresponding to the Pcdha, Pcdhb, and Pcdhg clusters are labelled below each distance map. Positions that gain H3K9me3 and those that do not are labeled by red and gray bars, respectively. Gray map regions denote missing polymer data.

Cells were then stained with RNA FISH probes targeting different Pcdha isoforms in the probe set. All transfected conditions showed mCherry signal (top panels), but FISH signal was observed only when the FISH probes targeted the same isoform that was expressed (bottom panels). (b) As in (a), but for Pcdhg isoforms. For (a,b), representative images from each transfection/FISH condition are shown. Multiple fields of view were examined for each condition, all with similar results. This validation experiment was performed once. Scale bars: 50 μm.

Sources indicate that (a) Example of Pcdh RNA staining for Pcdha6 and Pcdh DNA loci labelled by ORCA in the same cells. Insets show colocalization between Pcdha6 RNAs and Pcdh DNA loci. Images are from a representative field of view from one of two independent experiments with similar results. Scale bar: 10 μm. (b) Schematic of distance measurements used for nascent puncta analysis. For each Pcdh DNA locus, the 3D distance to the nearest RNA punctum was computed. (c) Histograms showing distributions of Pcdh DNA loci by 3D distance to the nearest RNA punctum for three representative Pcdh RNAs. Distances were calculated in 3D voxel coordinate space. Each distribution is bimodal, with a voxel distance of 8 separating proximal and distal populations; puncta within 8 voxel units of a DNA locus were classified as nascent. The threshold at 8 corresponds to a raw distance of 1.2 – 1.6 μm (see Methods for more details). (d) Intensities of RNA puncta within 8 voxels of a DNA locus versus puncta farther than 8 voxels from any locus, for the same Pcdh RNAs as in (c). Significance was assessed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Adjusted P values for Pcdha6, Pcdhb16, and Pcdhga1, respectively: P = 1.1 × 10−132, P = 2.7 × 10−58, and P = 7.3 × 10−23. Box plots show medians, interquartile ranges (box limits), notches representing approximate 95% confidence intervals for the median, and whiskers extending to non-outlier extrema within 1.5x the interquartile range. Outliers are not shown.

(d) Distribution of median STORM signal around randomly positioned loci across 1000 simulations compared to the median STORM signal around observed Tex15 sites. The median STORM signal around Pcdh DNA loci from Fig. 2c is also shown. Statistical significance was assessed using a one-sided empirical Monte Carlo test. The P value was calculated as the fraction of simulations with median STORM signal greater than or equal to the observed median. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied. (e) Mirrored distributions of local H3K9me3 STORM signal around Pcdh DNA loci and Tex15 nascent sites. STORM signal was measured within the same local radius used in (d) and is plotted as log10(STORM signal + 1). Transcription probability as a function of enhancer–promoter distance. Points indicate the fraction of promoter observations classified as transcribing within each bin. Data were aggregated across 28 Pcdh enhancer–promoter pairs included in the analysis and 16,399 ORCA traces from mOSNs. Gray bars indicate the number of promoter-to-enhancer measurements per bin. Bin size: 50 nm. Error bars: 95% Wilson binomial confidence intervals around the observed fraction in each bin.

(a) Left: schematic of distance measurements between locus positions and heterochromatin/euchromatin domain centres. For each locus position, dHC − dEC was calculated, where dHC and dEC are distances to the heterochromatin and cluster-specific euchromatin centres, respectively. Negative values indicate greater proximity to the heterochromatin centre; positive values indicate greater proximity to the euchromatin centre. Right: median per-trace dHC − dEC across locus positions in the Pcdhb and Pcdhg clusters for Pcdhb16-transcribing traces with enhancer–promoter contact, Pcdhb16-transcribing traces without enhancer–promoter contact, and non-transcribing Pcdhb16 traces. Vertical dashed lines: Pcdhb16 and its enhancer HS18-22. Red and gray bars: heterochromatic and euchromatic regions, respectively. n: traces per condition. (b) Change in dHC and dEC for Pcdhb16 and HS18-22 in Pcdhb16-transcribing traces with enhancer–promoter contact relative to transcribing traces without enhancer–promoter contact. Schematics illustrate promoter and enhancer positioning relative to the heterochromatin and euchromatin centres in non-contacting (no e–p) and contacting (e–p) states. (c) Median promoter dHC − dEC in transcribing traces without and with enhancer–promoter contact. Each paired set of points represents one Pcdh isoform. For each isoform, dHC − dEC was calculated per trace, then summarized as the median across traces in each contact state. (d) Median enhancer dHC − dEC in transcribing traces without and with enhancer–promoter contact, calculated as in (c). For (c,d), paired points correspond to the same Pcdh isoform or cognate enhancer. Significance was assessed using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P = 1.9 × 10−6 and P = 2.6 × 10−5 for (c,d), respectively. 30 Pcdh isoforms were included in the analysis. Arrowheads indicate c-type Pcdh genes or their enhancers. (e) Percent of transcribing traces with and without enhancer–promoter contact for each Pcdh isoform. For all panels, 16,399 ORCA traces from mOSNs were examined; only traces where the relevant promoters and enhancers were detected were included.

(c) H3K9me3 nChIP-seq over the Pcdh locus in four WT (Omp-GFP) and three Setdb1cKO biological replicates. Data were generated across two independent experiments. The two additional WT replicates in Fig. 5c are shown in Fig. 1h. (d) Top: median distance of each locus position to the heterochromatin (HC) domain centre in Rad21cKO and WT mOSNs. (g,h) Change in percent of mOSNs expressing Pcdhb and Pcdhg genes relative to WT as a function of distance to cognate enhancers in Rad21cKO (g) and distance to the heterochromatin/euchromatin boundary at the Pcdhb/Pcdhg region in Setdb1cKO (h). (i,j) Percent of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh gene as a function of enhancer–promoter contact frequency in Rad21cKO (i) and Setdb1cKO (j). In (g-j), contact frequency was calculated for each Pcdh promoter and cognate enhancer. Dashed line in (j) indicates a linear fit to heterochromatic Pcdh genes, with Pearson correlation shown. (k) Model of Pcdh transcription from a megabase-scale heterochromatin domain. Pcdh enhancers lie outside the heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh promoters. Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion brings enhancers into the domain to engage promoters, with transcription initiating from within the domain. After promoter activation, transcription can proceed in the absence of enhancer—promoter engagement. Transcription reads through downstream Pcdha and Pcdhg genes residing within the heterochromatin domain, and domain-scale compaction is maintained.

Speared Hearts’ craziness goes on as Gorgie boys give Monaco something to drop off at Louvre

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that eight goals at Dens Park is one thing.
  • The price the Hearts fans might have to pay for such swashbuckling play was also demonstrated.
  • Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that eight goals at Dens Park is one thing. Going toe-to-toe with French aristocrats and being beaten, cruelly, at the death is quite another. Hearts’ growing reputation as the great entertainers was nevertheless burnished here in thrilling fashion.

The price the Hearts fans might have to pay for such swashbuckling play was also demonstrated. Defensive fragility was all too apparent, including at the end when substitute Mamadou Coulibaly brushed off a challenge in midfield and threaded the ball through for Folarin Balogun to score his second and the night’s decisive goal. We were already into the final minute of the four added on at the end of a quite breathless European tie.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It has been revealed that mon Dieu! What a match. AS Monaco won’t forget this trip to Scotland, and a vibrant Tynecastle, in a hurry. As for the hosts, they remain just about alive in the Conference League.

The point they were deprived in heartbreaking fashion would have made such a difference. As good as Monaco are, it wasn’t as if Hearts were undone by a moment of genius, which makes it harder to bear. The hosts also had chances to score their own third goal and were angered when referee Daniel Schlager waved away penalty appeals when substitute Josh McPake ended up in a heap after Jordan Teze’s challenge.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the home supporters will simply have to put up with see-sawing emotions in a season that’s already shaping up to be one of the craziest in the club’s history. Perhaps defensive slackness, although costly, must simply be endured if goals continue to flow at the other end, especially ones as sensational as Hearts fans were treated to here. Drop them off in the Louvre on your way home, Monaco.

It has been revealed that jordi Altena’s opener was declared a “potential” goal of the season by the always judicious Tynecastle Tannoy announcer. Just as well because a better one was just around the corner. Sabah Kerjota’s curler on the stroke of half time was an immaculate finish that Lukas Hradecky, the experienced keeper, just had to stand rooted to his spot and admire.

Altena’s strike was not quite in the same unsavable part of the goal but it was still breathtaking in its execution. Kerjota, the little Albanian livewire, also played a part in it. His free-kick looked to be going in until Hradecky pushed the ball against the post. Claudio Braga made sure the ball was recycled and played it back to Kerjota, who passed it inside to Altena. The Dutchman is fast becoming a Tynecastle favourite. No wonder when he can strike a ball like this. Hradecky was left flapping at the air beneath his bar.

Since going 5-0 down to Falkirk after 47 minutes earlier this month at Tynecastle, Hearts had scored 10 unanswered goals. This was the 11th. The response was always coming. This was AS Monaco after all. They might be struggling right now in Ligue 1 but how can they be they be written off? The team remains packed full of talent. This was not the shadow side Hearts might have hoped to face. Eric Dier, the England international, was present and correct as was former Arsenal player – and Donald Trump’s friend - Balogun.

According to recent reports, monaco were the ones raising a quizzical French eyebrow at the home team sheet. Due to much publicised injury problems and lack of adequate club-trained academy players, Hearts couldn’t even fill the bench.

Industry observers note that matthew Gillies stepped in for his first senior start in midfield. Unless Monaco were familiar with Stenhousemuir's opening matches of this season, the talented 19-year-old might have been something of a mystery to them. The same applies to Finlay Pollock, who is something of a mystery to Hearts fans as well.

Industry observers note that pollock came on towards the end for his first Hearts appearance since 2024. The 22-year-old has been out on loan at East Fife and Raith Rovers in between times. He was given the last nine minutes in place of a drained Kerjota. The whole team, including substitutes, looked shattered at the end but they had contributed to a game that will live long in the memory. There was the drama of an overturned penalty for Hearts in the second half after an alleged handball by substitute Mathys Detourbet as well as the sight of Beau Reus galloping up field for a corner in the final seconds.

The visitors’ first goal of the night saw Balogun do the necessary – and no more - from the penalty spot after Stuart Findlay had clipped the heels of the dangerous Matthis Abline.

Sources indicate that there was some dismay among home fans about Reus’ lack of movement. Balogun’s penalty lacked conviction and certainly wasn’t placed in the corner. Far from it. Nevertheless, it brought Monaco level. The French side took heart although they didn’t have it all their own way. Abline was booked for a foul on Laurent Mendy as Hearts forced the visitors into sometimes desperate measures.

According to recent reports, monaco did though take the lead for the first time in the night five minutes before half time after Edan Diop took advantage of a slack ball from Altena following a throw-in. After playing a one-two with Balogun, he slipped the ball beyond Reus.

It has been revealed that gillies was showing his worth in midfield. He might have had a goal to tell his pals about had Pierre Landry Kabore not taken the ball off his foot as he was preparing to unleash a shot from the edge of the box. Kabore, following his brace against Dundee, was in frisky form but often got a little too excited and forgot the basics, such as avoiding running into teammates.

Gillies was withdrawn at half time for Blair Spittal, back from injury and desperate to play a part. He also took the captain’s armband from McCart and helped drive Hearts on. Sadly, his and others’ efforts were in vain on an agonising night for the hosts.

This one was not a match for the football connoisseur – but was one for fans of never-say-die defending as Broadbridge Heath put on a tenacious display of defending against promotion hopefuls Erith Town on a bitter cold Tuesday evening at the JM Clark Stadium.

Chris Simmons’ Heath side knew it would be a difficult match up against a Dockers side on top form, second in the division with games in-hand and with the best home record in the division having played eight and won all eight.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

But it was the Bears who had the first shot on target on 9 minutes when Sam Hards was brought down some 30 yards from goal and Ben Royall stepped up to take the resulting free-kick – hitting a left foot shot that was saved comfortably low to his left by the Dockers goalkeeper Javern Pitterson.

On 16 minutes Erith were awarded a free-kick wide on the right and just outside the penalty area, James Dyer played the ball into the danger area where it pinged in and around the 6 yard box before being cleared by Brad Peters and that set the tone for the first half with the hosts having most of the play but unable to break down the solid Bears defence.

Broadbridge Heath did have a few chances, Royall tried to catch Pitterson out with a shot to the near-post but the keeper got back to gather and Ollie Rawlins had a left foot shot saved by Pitterson diving low to his left and it was 0-0 at the break.

The Dockers stepped up a gear in the second half, kicking down the slope, and had the Bears pinned back in their own half for long periods but without really troubling goalkeeper Alfie Hadfield, plenty of goal attempts but everyone charged down by a Broadbridge Heath player defending like their lives depended on it.

On 75 minutes a rare foray deep into the Erith half saw Charlie Connell brought down by a clumsy challenge some 25 yards from goal, Ben Royal stepped up to take the resulting free-kick striking a left foot shot that deflected off the wall wrong-footing Pitterson who could do nothing but watch the ball fly into the net out of his reach.

The hosts continued to push players forward in search of an equaliser but just couldn’t get past the Broadbridge Heath defensive lines who stood firm and dealt with everything the Dockers could throw at them – and it remained 0-1 at the final whistle with Heath continuing their remarkable run of having scored in every league game this season.

Simmons remarked afterwards: “This one was a bit of a smash and grab, Erith are a very good side and should of gone in front in the first half, defensively we were excellent and our shape and organisation was top notch and in the end got the lucky break the lads deserved.”.

Next up for the Bears is the visit of division leaders Faversham Town to the Air Engineering Stadium on Saturday.

BBH: Hadfield, Cotton, Royall, Marino, Peters, Richardson, Connell, Bejashvili (Doughty 71), Rawlins, Holden, Hards.

Wouter Vrancken has stressed Hearts’ objective remains the same despite conceding a last-minute goal that led to an agonising defeat against AS Monaco at Tynecastle.

Hearts’ hopes of reaching the knockout stage rest on winning their last two Conference League matches against Bosnian side Borac Banja Luca and Cypriot team Pafos, probably by high-scoring margins.

The Tynecastle manager was not giving up on anything after the 3-2 loss, with United States World Cup star Folarin Balogun scoring the winning goal in the final seconds of added time.

It has been revealed that hearts had taken the lead after a sensational strike from Jordi Altena on 15 minutes. A penalty from Balogun levelled things before the visitors took the lead with a goal from Edam Diop five minutes before half time. Sabah Kerjota scored the goal of the night on the stroke of half-time after curling in with his left foot to leave everything to play for in the second half.

Sources indicate that “I think the point doesn't make a difference,” mentioned Vrancken. “There's also something that really was pleasing for me is that when it was 2-2, we still wanted to go (for the win).

"You saw also when it was a throw-in, we wanted to do it fast, we wanted to go for the win. Against a side like this, in the situation we're in, I am so really proud of this also.

In a recent development, "Three points would make a difference," he added. "Zero or one point doesn't make a difference towards the next games, so you have to win the next games. One point or no points doesn't change anything in the next games.”.

Sources indicate that the Belgian stressed his pride in his players and reiterated that Hearts were missing nine injured players as well as Leart Kabashi and Eduardo Ageu, who were not named in the European squad. He did, however, lament the lack of concentration that saw them concede so late in the game after 93-and-a-half minutes of lung-busting effort. He was also unhappy that Hearts were not cute enough to stop Monaco in their tracks as they broke free for the winning goal. Substitute Finlay Pollock had the chance to clip Mamadou Coulibaly’s heels before the midfielder played in Balogun. Ruthlessness might be something Hearts are lacking at this level. A reporter pointed out that it was a cruel way to lose a match.

Recent findings suggest that “It did feel like this,” said Vrancken. “But at the same time, we have to learn in that situation because I think until then we were really solid about giving chances away. And I expect more from guys who come in from the side (substitutes).

“We can win it with a fresh player and in the middle we can win it with a fresh player. Or you make a foul somewhere to keep the result - I expect this. This is like battling for the team, as I call it.

Industry observers note that “We have to do better there,” he added. “But the biggest thing, of course, is to be really proud of what performance we put on the park today, because it's against a really good side. Knowing that we have still nine injuries - I will name it - and we have a lot of players not on the European list today and still do this against that team. I'm really proud of what we did.”.

Sources indicate that he hailed the quality of his side’s goals. “You see also the confidence those guys have. This is what we wanted after the weekend, of course - that you take some confidence from the dynamics of what we did there. I think the conviction around the box was there, in both boxes actually. It's an important thing to take with us towards the next games coming, especially in this run of games.”.

Sources indicate that hearts host Celtic, who beat them 7-1 last month, at Tynecastle on Sunday. Vrancken is firmly in the belief that his side have their mojo back following this and the 5-2 defeat to Falkirk earlier this month. Hearts have since beaten Dundee 8-0 and been edged out by Monaco in a five-goal thriller. “We have played two good games and two good performances against good sides, especially today,” he said. “And now you have the confidence. But we are still playing against a good side on Sunday with only two days' rest, so we have to manage fatigue and make sure that we are as fresh as possible again to make up for something a few weeks ago, especially because it's an at-home game.”.

According to recent reports, monaco manager Filipe Luis, meanwhile, denied that relief was the primary emotion after leaving it so late to collect three points. “It is not relief, we compete to win,” he said. “We had an amazing opportunity to win tonight but we had a tough opponent.

“They scored two unbelievable goals,” he added. “You almost need to applaud them. When a team scores two goals like this it is almost nobody’s fault. They are two fantastic goals. Honestly, it’s very beautiful.”.

Industry observers note that he spoke admiringly of the atmosphere. “I played against Celtic (with Atletico Madrid) in 2011 I think in the Europa League,” he noted. “We are lucky to have the opportunity to play these types of games in different countries. It is so intense. I am happy to have had this opportunity to be here tonight – and happy with the result.”.

  • Winless against Lorient in two years, Paris Saint-Germain welcome the 10th-placed visitors to Parc des Princes for Saturday's matchday 12 clash.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 09:45.

Winless against Lorient in two years, Paris Saint-Germain welcome the 10th-placed visitors to Parc des Princes for Saturday's matchday 12 clash.

The defending Ligue 1 champions' 12-match winning streak was halted by Roma on Wednesday, but they now aim to extend their sequence of eight consecutive top-flight victories.

PSG had maintained a perfect record across all competitions for nearly three months before Roma visited in the Champions League in midweek, with the Serie A side battling to a 2-2 draw on matchday five.

That result ended the Parisians' four-match European winning streak, although Luis Enrique's men remain second in the league-phase standings and firmly inside the coveted top-eight places that guarantee last-16 qualification.

Returning to league action should please supporters, who have watched their side claim eight consecutive victories since losing to Monaco at the start of September, albeit with only three clean sheets.

However, eagle-eyed observers will note that the Red and Blues have won only one of their last five meetings with Lorient across the past four years, with three of the last four encounters ending level.

Another draw would please Paris FC, Lille and Lyon, who trail the capital club by three, five and six points respectively as the Ligue 1 title race begins to take shape.

Alexandre Dujeux therefore aims to prevent Lorient's first defeat in this fixture since April 2024; however, his own five-match winless record against PSG and four consecutive losses to Enrique are ominous signs for the 50-year-old manager.

An indifferent run of results further undermines confidence in Les Merlus extending their unbeaten sequence in this fixture, with the Brittany-based club winning only one of their last four league matches.

Admittedly, only one of those matches ended in defeat, a 2-0 home loss to Brest, while their solitary victory during that period came away at Le Havre.

However, that early-November success offers limited encouragement given that it came against the division's bottom side, who have collected a paltry two points from 11 matches.

Their overall away record is more encouraging, with Dujeux's team conceding just twice across five matches on the road, both in September's 2-1 defeat to Le Mans, while keeping clean sheets in the other four.

Another shutout would make Lorient the first team since Monaco in November last year to prevent PSG from scoring, a feat far easier mentioned than done.

Paris Saint-Germain Ligue 1 form:.

Paris Saint-Germain form (all competitions):.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue are both sidelined with ACL injuries for PSG's fixture on Saturday.

Ousmane Dembele and Marquinhos are pushing for their first starts since last month's 4-2 victory over Barcelona, although Enrique may be tempted to retain the centre-back partnership of Ilya Zabarnyi and Willian Pacho.

Ferran Torres remains the capital club's leading Ligue 1 scorer with five goals, while Achraf Hakimi, Senny Mayulu and Marquinhos have three apiece.

Lorient have shared the goals around this season, with nine different players finding the net for the Brittany-based visitors.

Only Jean-Victor Makengo has scored more than once for Les Merlus, leaving Dujeux searching for someone to step up at Parc des Princes.

The visitors' prospects are further weakened by the absence of Panos Katseris, with a muscle injury ruling their leading goal provider out of this weekend's encounter.

Isaak Toure (groin) and Bandiougou Fadiga (muscle) are also sidelined for the 10th-placed side on matchday 12.

Paris Saint-Germain possible starting lineup:.

Safonov; Hakimi, Pacho, Marquinhos, Mendes; Zaire-Emery, Vitinha, Ruiz; Akliouche, Dembele, Godts.

Lorient possible starting lineup:.

Mvogo; Adjei, Talbi, Obaretin; Sylla, Cadiou, Ebong, Kouassi; Makengo, Bernardeau; Tosin.

Lorient's four clean sheets from five away matches suggest that PSG may need patience, particularly against opponents who have repeatedly frustrated them in recent meetings.

However, the visitors' limited scoring threat and Katseris's absence should allow Enrique's men to sustain pressure and eventually secure a ninth consecutive league victory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Colombian’s late header ends Celtic’s 23-year Portuguese hoodoo in gritty Torreense triumph.

Celtic clinched a vital 2-1 Europa League victory over second-tier outfit Torreense, thanks to an 84th-minute header from substitute Camilo Duran that ended the Scottish champions' 23-and-a-half-year wait for an away win on Portuguese soil.

It has been revealed that played nearly 50 miles away from Torreense’s 2,431-capacity home at Estadio Manuel Marques, which fails to meet UEFA stadium criteria, the 24,000-seater Municipal Stadium in Leiria was dominated by roughly 4,000 travelling Celtic supporters, making up two-thirds of the crowd. Despite the partisan backing, Martin O’Neill’s men made remarkably hard work of overcoming a side sitting 13th in Portugal’s second division with just two league wins from their opening ten matches.

There is an old adage in European football that fortunes earned by accident are rarely retained by design. For 45 disjointed minutes, Celtic offered a textbook demonstration of the principle. Handed an early advantage through the sort of comical defending usually reserved for Scottish clubs on their continental travels, Martin O’Neill’s side promptly retreated into their shell, allowing Portuguese second-tier minnows Torreense to restore parity and seize the initiative before the interval.

Celtic’s precarious Europa League campaign was balanced on a knife-edge. Having opened their league-phase campaign with three consecutive defeats before salvaging a breathless 3-2 victory over Beşiktaş in Glasgow earlier this month, O’Neill’s men arrived in central Portugal languishing in 32nd place.

Anything less than maximum points against a Torreense side operating in the lower reaches of Liga Portugal 2, yet remarkably seated 19th in this competition with six points following last season’s improbable Taça de Portugal triumph, threatened to render Celtic’s remaining fixtures against Omonia, Marseille, and Union Saint-Gilloise an exercise in mathematical futility.

It has been revealed that O’Neill had cautioned on the eve of the tie that his squad lacked the pedigree to indulge in complacency. Initially, however, the evening appeared set to unfold with uncharacteristic smoothness for the Scottish champions.

Recent findings suggest that restored to the European squad as an injury replacement for Mika Baur, Jota marked his return to his homeland with immediate industry down the left flank. Inside nine minutes, the winger collected possession near the by-line and whipped a low, enticing delivery into the six-yard box. With Yang Hyun-jun hovering intently at the back post, Torreense full-back Javi Vázquez panicked under pressure, slicing his attempted clearance past his own goalkeeper and into the net.

Industry observers note that it was a moment of extreme generosity, yet Celtic proved remarkably ungrateful recipients. Rather than using their early cushion to assert authority, the visitors lapsed into a passive, defensive shell. Though Celtic commanded the majority of possession, they managed to invite pressure rather than alleviate it.

Sources indicate that torreense, a club steeped in modest provincial history rather than continental glamour, sensed the vulnerability. Vázquez nearly atoned for his earlier mistake in the 17th minute with a venomous, low free-kick from a narrow angle that required hasty defensive intervention. Two minutes later, the equaliser duly arrived, born of Celtic’s chronic inability to clear their lines.

It has been revealed that given acres of space 20 yards from goal, midfielder Álex Alfaro unleashed a fierce drive that crashed against the underside of Sam Johnstone’s crossbar. As the ball dropped invitingly inside the penalty area, Celtic’s backline froze. Kieran Tierney’s tentative, lofted clearance succeeded only in teeing up Dany Jean, and the forward exhibited admirable composure to dart past Colby Donovan and drill a low finish beyond Johnstone’s reach.

Recent findings suggest that jota remained Celtic’s sole reliable source of invention. Celtic’s solitary threat to reclaim the lead prior to the break arrived on the stroke of half-time, when the Portuguese star's deep cross was hooked back across the face of goal by Luke McCowan, only for Kasper Høgh to arrive a fraction too late to apply the finishing touch.

It has been revealed that jota nearly restored the lead within seconds of the restart, only for his attempted dink to be gathered by a scrambling Adriel. But as the hour mark approached, Celtic’s frustration grew.

Former Hearts striker Musa Drammeh nearly dealt a massive blow to their hopes of progressing to the knockout stages by shrugging off a feeble challenge before dragging a golden chance narrowly wide of the far post.

Sources indicate that james Forrest took over from the impressive Jota in the closing stages and the substitution proved to be a masterstroke. With Celtic seemingly sleepwalking toward a damaging result, Forrest swung a pinpoint cross in from the right, and Duran peeled away at the back post to power a downward header past Adriel. It was the Colombian’s 15th goal of a remarkable campaign, once again rescuing his side.

McCowan missed a late one-on-one opportunity to add a touch of gloss to the scoreline in the 89th minute, seeing his tame finish saved by Adriel’s boot. However, it did not matter. For the first time since O’Neill’s side triumphed at Boavista in April 2003, Celtic left Iberian soil victorious.
